grades.quote: Multiple page table entries can point to the same page frame. In the extreme case, an entire virtual address space of 2<sup>64</sup> bytes could be made readable as zeros by having all the page table entries marked read-only and pointed at a single zeroed-out page frame.
grades.reason: Exercise text only. It notes that many page table entries can point to one page frame, so a huge virtual range needs little physical memory. It never explains sparse address spaces or how unmapped regions avoid using physical memory.
Describes the size and range of the LoongArch virtual address space (VALEN, LA32/LA64). It says nothing about sparse use or why physical memory use can be far smaller than the range.

grades.quote: The table need not contain a physical address translation for every page of virtual addresses; in effect, some entries can be left blank. These undefined virtual addresses are illegal for the processor to use.
grades.reason: Gives the core mechanism. The mapping table need not have entries for every virtual page, so unmapped parts of the address space use no physical memory. Translations are created only on demand.

grades.quote: The simplest example of memory-conserving sharing occurs when multiple processes are running the same program.
grades.reason: Covers a different reason virtual size can exceed physical use: shared physical memory such as program text and libraries is mapped into several processes. It does not address sparse address spaces directly.
